first_prompt: Work on the brief in `llm-dlc/loops/sync-performance.md`. Read it in full now, even if you have read it before: it is the instruction for this cycle and every cycle of this loop, and what you remember

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 1: per-command timings, each snapshot read once by check, global files rebuilt once per sync, no Langfuse in commit, linear email matching; equivalent rules keep their stamp
commits.body:
First changeset of llm-dlc/loops/sync-performance.md. Every sync.py command appends its timings to ~/.local/state/llm-traces/perf.jsonl: wall and CPU time per phase, bytes, cache misses, subprocesses and network requests. 'sync.py perf' shows them. check decompresses each stored snapshot once and shows an older log is a prefix of the current one by hashing the current log's first bytes, instead of decompressing every older log again. write_index runs once per sync instead of once per session. Generated files are written only when they change. store_log takes sizes from the bytes in hand and compresses at level 6 (on a 79 MB log, 1.25 s against 1.66 s at level 9, for 0.6% more bytes; identifiers hash the uncompressed bytes, so none change). Commit and sync no longer contact Langfuse: the Stop hook already sends finished turns at the end of every turn, and now reads nothing when Langfuse is not configured. 'sync.py langfuse SID' sends a session's turns by hand. In redaction_rules.py, email_spans finds exactly what EMAIL_RE found, in linear time; EMAIL_RE was quadratic on long runs of address characters and was the costliest rule on real logs. env-secret, the second costliest, gets a cheap exact pre-test.

Measured with Langfuse, wrangler and the CDN stubbed. Same repository state, old against new code: check 126.4 s to 106.5 s, with 5.46 GB decompressed down to 2.47 GB; sync of all 19 sessions 78.1 s to 61.6 s; push's work after its sync (check, upload of 3 outstanding objects, check) 229.7 s to 212.2 s. Scanning, not decompression as the review assumed, is about 85% of check's CPU, and most of what is left. Commit still syncs every session and the 'live' rule still goes by modification time; both are for the next changeset, along with a scan cache keyed by content and batched jj reads (202 'jj file show' calls per check).

Stamp: the speed-ups give the same results as the stamped rules, so the stamp keeps its date. A new 'sync.py stamp --equivalent' compares the edited rules with the stamped ones at @- on every distinct line of every transcript, stored log and published file (76,799 lines): redaction, and findings before and after it. It writes the new hash with the old date only if nothing differs, and here nothing did. A plain 'sync.py stamp' now refuses only on open errors; open warnings become allow-list proposals, which check reports as warnings until a person approves or drops them. Five such proposals are open: four made-up test values written into this session's transcript (the files now build them at run time), and a placeholder Windows home directory in session 2e359813. None needs action before a push.

commits.summary: Sync-performance brief: instructions that keep the loop running, and the progress of earlier runs
commits.body: The feature loop stops when a cycle ends without a commit, when the decision turn lacks a clear LOOP line, or when the brief changes. Last cycle nearly stopped for minor reasons: a denied commit, a stamp refused over warning-level findings from made-up test values, and a question about a policy the brief could have settled. A new section, Keep the loop running, says to end every cycle with a commit (the largest unblocked part, the rest deferred), to take the conservative choice and record it rather than pause for minor questions, to adapt after a denied command, to keep network side effects out of commit, sync and check, to keep the stamp for equivalent rules edits (stamp --equivalent), to treat findings in one's own log as allow-list proposals, to run long jobs in the background, and to continue when in doubt. Each run counts only its own commits, so a Progress section records that the first changeset is done (rxowqurq, with its measurements) and that the next run starts on the second. Without it, a new run would have redone the first. The Langfuse section notes the user's decision, the stamp note in section 3 points to stamp --equivalent, and test_performance.py joins the test list. No code changed.

commits.summary: langfuse-loop.sh: send unsent turns to Langfuse as they appear
commits.body: sync.py langfuse gains --pending (sessions whose latest stored log has turns not yet sent; a state-file mark by log sha keeps the check cheap) and --all (send them). llm-dlc/tools/langfuse-loop.sh polls that list, runs --all, retries while Langfuse is down, and takes stop/now/? commands like verification-loop.sh, with no Claude session. Verified against the local Langfuse: 19 pending sessions sent, then the loop idles on 'nothing to send'.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2a: commit redacts only what a transcript gained, check scans only logs it has not scanned
commits.body:
Two local caches in ~/.local/state/llm-traces/ keep commit and check from redoing work, without changing what either produces or reports (llm-dlc/specification.md, new section Local caches). transcript-cache.json records, per transcript, how many bytes were redacted into which stored log. The redactor works line by line, so the log of a longer transcript is that log's first part plus the redaction of what was appended. The part is reused only if the transcript's first bytes still hash to the recorded SHA-256 and the stored log still holds its name's content; an unfinished last line is redacted on its own. scan-cache.json records what scanning each stored log found, keyed by the SHA-256 check computes from its content (not its name), as finding ids, masked values and counts, never values. A new snapshot is scanned only past the longest earlier log of its session that is a prefix of it. The session's summary, manifest, metrics and notes files go through the same cache by content. Reviewed findings and the allow list are applied afterwards, as before. Every entry is under a fingerprint of redaction_rules.py, sync.py, the Python version and a hash of this machine's literals; any change empties the cache. --full on sync and check, or LLM_TRACES_FULL=1, trusts nothing cached: the full audit.

Measured on the same state (sync.py perf): check 106.5 s before; 100.9 s with a cold cache (first run after any change to either tool); 14.3 s warm, of which 6.5 s is decompressing and 1.3 s hashing all 161 snapshots, 4.4 s the 206 jj file show calls for trailers and 1.7 s metrics. sync (the work of commit) 62.7 s cold, 4.7 s warm, nothing redacted again: the rest is 1.8 s of jj log calls linking commits and 0.6 s of summaries. Within one run, prefix reuse already cuts the text scanned from 2.07 GB to 0.41 GB, but the cold run stays at 85 s because the cost is in the 45,000 distinct lines, not in repeats: only the cache across runs removes it.

Verified: check output identical to the old code's before and after a sync, cold and warm. Incremental and full redaction give identical logs for all 23 real transcripts (173 MB) cut at random points, and decoding matches Path.read_text. Seven new tests in test_performance.py (now 26) cover growing made-up transcripts with every line break and invalid UTF-8, a rewritten transcript, a damaged stored log, fingerprints and --full, cached scans judged like fresh ones, and a log whose content no longer matches its name. test_review.py and test_metrics.py pass. Tests now keep their caches and measurements in a temporary directory.

Still open in the second changeset: verifying snapshots by content on every check (7.8 s), reading trailers and historical manifests in one batch (4.4 s), linking commits with fewer jj calls, an explicit session for commit, scan/review/stamp reusing the transcript cache (review still redacts every transcript, about 2 minutes), and commit validating what it changed so that a separate check is not needed. A made-up TEST-NET address typed in a draft test got into this session's log; it is proposed for the allow list (37f924ec) and warns in check until approved.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2b: check verifies a snapshot once by its .gz bytes, and reads every trailer's manifest in one git call
commits.body:
A warm check took 14.7 s, nearly all of it repeated work on unchanged content: 6.6 s decompressing all 161 stored snapshots (2.48 GB) and 1.4 s hashing them to show they match their names, 1.7 s rendering every session's metrics again to compare with metrics.json, and 4.6 s on 206 separate `jj file show` calls for the manifest committed with each trailer. The same check now takes 0.9 s (14.7 s before, measured with `sync.py perf` on the same state). It decompresses 32 MB instead of 2.48 GB, and makes one `git cat-file --batch` call instead of 206 jj calls. A cold run, after any edit to sync.py, takes 97 s, against 101 s before.

How: a third local cache, ~/.local/state/llm-traces/check-cache.json (CheckCache), holds what check works out from content, each under the SHA-256 of exactly that content. A snapshot's entry is keyed by the hash of its .gz bytes and records the hash and length of what they decompress to. Decompression is deterministic, so a file read before is verified against its name with no need to decompress it again, while any change to its bytes means it is decompressed and hashed afresh. Its .gz bytes are kept in memory and decompressed only if a scan or the metrics need the content, never re-read from disk. The digests of the current log's prefixes are kept by its content. Whether metrics.json matches is kept under a key built from the content of its logs, the manifest, the file itself and pricing.json; the fingerprint adds metrics.py to the redactor's (both tools' source, the Python version, this machine's literals). `check --full` trusts none of it. The manifests in historical trees come from `tree_files`, one `git cat-file --batch` over the colocated store. A commit git lacks, or a missing git, falls back to `jj file show` for that commit.

Verified: the output of check (all 30 notes, 2 warnings, 0 errors) is identical, byte for byte, across the old code, the new code with a cold cache, with a warm cache, and with --full. test_performance.py has 30 tests (4 new in Checks) and passes, as do test_review.py and test_metrics.py. The new tests cover the following. A warm check runs with decompression and prefix hashing disabled and gives the same result. A snapshot recompressed differently still verifies. Other content under a name is an error and is compared by its bytes. A current log rewritten under its name gets its prefixes worked out for what it holds. Metrics are compared again when the logs, the manifest, metrics.json or the price list change, and not otherwise. tree_files agrees with `jj file show` on real commits, including missing paths, a directory and an unknown commit.

Correction to the brief: it proposes caching historical manifest validation by git commit SHA and session. Once the reads are batched, all 206 take 0.08 s, so a cache would save almost nothing and add a way to be wrong. It was not added. Still open in the second changeset: fewer jj calls when linking commits, an explicit session identity for commit, scan/review/stamp using the transcript cache, commit-time validation in place of a separate check, and a final publication gate.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2c: commit syncs only the sessions whose inputs or outputs changed
commits.body:
A commit used to sync all 20 sessions in the project directory: each one's transcript checked against the transcript cache (decompressing its stored log to verify it), three jj log calls each, its summary and metrics rendered again. Now sync without session names (and so commit) skips a session whose state equals the one recorded right after its last sync, in a new local file, ~/.local/state/llm-traces/sync-cache.json. The state is everything process() reads or writes for that session, read cheaply: size, mtime and inode of its transcript and subagent transcripts (taken before reading, so a later write shows), the SHA-256 of its manifest, summary, metrics and note, its stored log names, its status, and every change that link_commits stamps or lists for it (those with its LLM-Trace line, and mutable ones authored within 120 s of its span, with description, emptiness, whether it is @, and the git SHA once immutable). One jj log call reads that for all sessions. The cache's fingerprint covers both tools, the rules and local literals, metrics.py, the summary template, pricing, reviewed findings, the allow list and the remote URL. Skipping is conservative: a publish always syncs everything and records no state (it writes git SHAs a normal sync leaves out), and sync --all or --full syncs every session. The session running the command is now always current, by CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, as well as any transcript written in the last 10 minutes as before.

Measured on this repo, with warm caches: the old commit took 5.1 s (20 sessions processed, 60 jj log calls, 155 MB decompressed). An incremental sync now takes 0.7 s (1 session processed, 19 unchanged, 5 jj log calls, 12.5 MB decompressed), against 5.6 s for sync --all. That meets the brief's 'Done when' for commit: the work follows the session that changed, not how many sessions exist. Equivalence: after the incremental sync, sync --all changed none of the 216 files belonging to the other 19 sessions and none of the 117 commit descriptions. The only changes were the two global rollups, which count the growing current session. A test also checks that the 120 s margin covers jj's own made revset for every real session. New tests (Incremental, 4) cover skipping, transcript growth, a hand-edited summary, a new note, a status change, a named session, the full audit, a changed tool, a publish, and which commit changes count. test_performance (34), test_review and test_metrics pass. The specification's Local caches section (now four files) and its On a commit paragraph, and the usage text, describe this.

Brief corrections: its Progress section still says 'Next: the second changeset', but steps 2a and 2b (zwzolxqo, qpqnrsym) and this one are done. Also, any edit to sync.py voids the transcript cache, because its fingerprint covers sync.py's source. So the first commit after such an edit redacts every transcript again (about 65 s). That is the conservative choice and is kept.

Deferred for the user: whether a commit should make only the committing session current. Today any other session whose transcript changed in the last 10 minutes also stamps @ with its LLM-Trace line, which marks files another live agent left in @ as its work. Narrowing that would change which commits carry which sessions' traces, a change in what is published, so the old rule is kept alongside the explicit identity.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2d: commit checks what it committed, so agents run no separate check
commits.body:
sync.py commit now ends by running the same check as sync.py check on what it just committed. It reuses the redactor from its own sync and the local caches, so the check only rescans what the commit added. Errors and warnings are printed as before. Notes are only counted, since they need no action. The command fails if the check finds an error, but the commit stands, as it did when the check was a separate step: the fix goes in a later commit. LLM_TRACES_FULL=1 makes the check trust no cache, as it does for the other commands. A plain jj commit traced by the hook is still not checked. CLAUDE.md, the procedure in llm-dlc/README.md, the specification's 'On a commit' paragraph, the usage text and the run-verification skill now describe this. A separate check is only needed to list the notes or after a plain jj commit.

Measured on this repo with warm caches (20 sessions, 163 snapshots): sync 0.9 s and the separate check 1.4 s, each in its own process. The commit's own timing is in its perf record (sync.py perf 1 commit). The first run after editing sync.py is cold, as before: sync 67 s, check 98 s. That is the same total as the old commit followed by check, because the tool's fingerprint empties the caches.

Verified: test_performance.py 36 tests (2 new: commit runs describe, sync, jj new, then the check with its sync's redactor and notes counted, and fails exactly when the check does; a check with notes not listed prints the same errors and warnings and counts the notes), test_review.py and test_metrics.py pass. Warnings: the open allow-list proposal and public-ip 20…3 in this session's logs, now also in snapshot 97d0bcfb6a4c. That is the value already proposed as 37f924ec, so it needs only the user's decision on that proposal.

Brief correction: its Progress section still lists only the first changeset. Steps 2a-2d of the second changeset are now done in this run (zwzolxqo, qpqnrsym, sqkxtqkv and this commit).

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2e: push verifies the exact revision it publishes before jj git push
commits.body:
The brief's second changeset asks for a final publication gate that validates the exact resulting revision. Until now push's second check read the trace files on disk, while jj git push publishes whatever the bookmark points at; nothing compared the two, and the specification's promise that no pushed commit points at a log nobody can fetch rested on upload having run, not on a check. publication_gate() closes both: it resolves the revisions the push would move bookmarks to (push_revisions(): those named by --bookmark/-b, including glob: patterns, -r, -c or --all, otherwise every bookmark not among the remote ones' ancestors, more than jj pushes by default and never less), lists each one's tree with one git ls-tree, and requires every tracked file where trace files live (llm-dlc/traces, llm-dlc/session-notes, the index and the two review lists) to be one that check read, with the same git blob id as the file on disk, and every file check read to be in the revision. It then reads the commits the push makes public (::targets ~ ::remote_bookmarks()) and requires each LLM-Trace line with a sha256 to name a log whose manifest records its CDN URL, or that was withdrawn. Any error prints and stops the push before git runs. It adds no network request.

Measured on this repo: the gate on @- takes 0.2 s for the whole process (one jj log, one git ls-tree, one jj log for the 8 unpushed commits, and hashing 63 files). It passed the tree comparison and reported, correctly, that the 10 trailers of the 8 commits not yet pushed name logs that are not uploaded, which a push uploads before it gets there. The 8 new PublicationGate tests in test_performance.py build commits with git plumbing in a temporary repository (write-tree and commit-tree, no git commit). They cover the checked revision passing, a file edited after the commit, a log and a stray session note committed where check never looked, a checked file missing from the revision, a trailer pointing at a log with no URL (withdrawn and legacy trailers pass), a revset jj cannot resolve, how push arguments become a revset, and push stopping before git when the gate fails. test_performance (44 tests), test_review and test_metrics pass. The specification's On a push and Storage paragraphs, the README's push line and the usage text describe the gate. Gap: the bookmark can still move between the gate and jj git push, since jj git push --bookmark takes no expected target; push holds no lock against another session for that moment.

Brief out of date: its Progress section still lists only the first changeset; steps 2a to 2e are this run's commits.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2f: scan, review and stamp read the transcript, scan and check caches
commits.body:
scan, review (with review show, review accept and allow propose/approve) and stamp redacted every transcript newer than the rules' stamp from scratch and scanned everything they publish, without reading the caches commit and check fill: review took 150 s and scan 147 s on this machine's 12 sessions, mostly redacting and scanning the 11 MB transcript of the session asking. Now a transcript is redacted only from where the log sync last stored for it ends (the transcript cache, read but never saved by these commands, since the log they make is not stored), and the redacted transcript, each stored log not yet uploaded and each session file is looked up in the scan cache by the SHA-256 of what it holds, scanned only if it is not there, or only past an earlier log of its session that is a prefix of it. A stored log is named through the check cache by its .gz bytes, as check does. What a preview scans is merged into the cache files, never replacing check's entries. Reviewed and allowed findings are applied afterwards, as for a fresh scan. --full on each command (or LLM_TRACES_FULL=1) trusts no cache; the old code path stays as scanned_findings.

Values: the scan cache holds finding ids and masked values only, which is all review, scan and stamp print or record (a stamp's allow-list proposals hold the masked value). A command that needs a finding's real value (review show, review accept, allow propose and approve) takes it from what this run scanned or from finding-values.json, used only if the finding's id is the hash of that kind and value, and reads everything again, the old way, if one is not known.

Measured with sync.py perf, after a sync and a check with this code: review 150.3 s to 0.9 s, scan 146.8 s to 0.9 s, review show 0.9 s; 136.7 MB of transcript not redacted again, 74 K characters redacted and 51 K scanned instead of 136.7 M and 145.7 M. review --full took 155.0 s and scan --full 148.2 s, as before. On the same state, review and review --full printed identical bytes; scan and scan --full differed only in the transcript sizes, since this session's transcript grew between the two runs, with the same marker counts and warnings. scan now prints sizes in bytes rather than characters. The measurement also caught a defect, fixed here: a --full preview saved only what it had scanned, dropping check's entries, and the next review took 16.3 s.

Tests: test_performance.Previews (5 new): findings from the caches equal reading everything, including reviewed findings left out and counted, and the transcript cache is not saved; values come from a scan, the remembered list (only when the id names them) or a full reread; scan prints what scan --full prints and scans nothing the second time; stamp proposes masked values from the caches; a --full preview drops no entry. test_performance (49), test_review (25) and test_metrics (21) pass. specification.md describes the preview commands under Local caches.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 2g: the Stop hook reads a transcript from a cursor at the first turn not yet sent
commits.body:
When Langfuse is configured, the end-of-turn hook (sync.py hook) redacted and parsed the whole transcript on every turn to find the turns not yet sent. Measured against a stubbed network on frozen copies (the transcript cut before its last prompt, then whole, then again): this 12 MB session took 5.88 s for one new turn and 5.71 s for none; the 94 MB transcript 41.75 s and 40.44 s, at 1.2 GB peak memory. Now 0.34 s and 0.02 s, and 0.24 s and 0.09 s. The hook keeps a cursor with the session's Langfuse state in ~/.local/state/llm-traces/: the byte offset of the first turn not yet sent (or of the unfinished last line), the SHA-256 of the bytes before it, the redactor's fingerprint, the number of turns before it and the last title there. It is used only when that prefix still hashes the same under the same rules and tools; a replaced or truncated transcript, or LLM_TRACES_FULL=1, reads the whole transcript, reusing the log sync last made where the transcript cache still applies (not saved). The cursor moves only after a send succeeds, and only over whole transcript lines: lines_in counts how many lines the redactor reads from each raw line (a carriage return or a raw U+2028 makes two), so the log is split at the same places. export_langfuse takes the number of the first turn, and it and langfuse send now keep the other keys of the state file (before, a hook export dropped the 'complete' mark langfuse --pending relies on), written atomically.

Verified: on both transcripts the request the new hook sends for the new turn is byte-identical to the committed code's (35 spans for turn 42 here, 1 for turn 209 there). New tests in test_performance.py (HookCursor, 5): over 12 seeds a made-up transcript grows in 10 steps with broken lines, CR and CRLF endings, raw U+2028, invalid UTF-8, lines cut mid-way and finished later, a transcript replaced under the same name and failed sends, and after each step the hook sends exactly what redacting and parsing everything sends (over 100 turns in all); the cursor makes it redact only what was appended; a changed prefix, LLM_TRACES_FULL=1 or other rules make it read everything; the state keeps its other keys; lines_in agrees with decoding and with the redactor. Dropping the turn numbering fails the first test. test_performance 54, test_review 25, test_metrics 21: all pass. The specification's end-of-turn entry describes the cursor. A first hook run after sync.py changes still reads the whole transcript once (47 s for the 94 MB one, as the transcript cache fingerprint also changed); after a commit it reuses that cache.

This finishes the second changeset. The brief's Progress section still says 'Next: the second changeset'; it was done in steps 2a to 2g of this run (the brief is not edited during a run).

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 3a: push uploads several logs at once, reuses check's scans, and keeps a durable upload record
commits.body:
First piece of the third changeset (persistent preparation and publication workers), on the upload path the review's section 6 describes. cmd_upload now hands each log to an Uploader in a thread pool: four logs at a time (LLM_TRACES_UPLOAD_JOBS), so their CDN reads overlap each other and the puts, with wrangler puts one at a time (LLM_TRACES_PUT_JOBS, default 1). Before a put, the stored .gz file is verified against the log's name through check's cache, and the log is scanned through check's scan cache. A log check has just scanned under the same rules is therefore not scanned again, and LLM_TRACES_FULL=1 reads and scans everything. Verifying first is new: the old loop would have put a file whose content did not match its name and only failed at the CDN read-back, after the wrong bytes were public. The read-back through the CDN after each put is unchanged, and each URL goes into its manifest as soon as it is verified. That includes uploads that finish while Ctrl-C is on its way out, so an interrupted push keeps what it verified.

The durable upload record (~/.local/state/llm-traces/uploads.json, mode 600, written through atomically) tells three states apart: never attempted (absent), attempted (written before the put: the object may be in R2), and verified (the CDN served its content). The next push names the logs an interrupted one may have uploaded. What gets uploaded is still decided by the manifests and a CDN lookup, which also cover other machines. unpublish removes the log's entry.

Groundwork for a single repository coordinator: every temporary file now comes from one atomic_write, used for logs, generated files, caches, the Langfuse state, finding values and the perf log. It names each file after the process, the thread and a random part, creates it exclusively (mode 600 from the first byte for private files), and removes it if the write fails. Before, names held only the pid, and finding-values.json used a fixed .tmp. Perf is now thread-safe, with a per-thread phase stack and locked counters. Also fixed: ScanCache and CheckCache bound their default paths at import, so the tests, which point those paths at a temporary directory, were overwriting this machine's real scan and check caches with test entries. They never trusted those entries, because the fingerprint differs, but each test run made the next real check run cold. The paths are now read when a cache is created, and a test run leaves the real files untouched (checked by mtime).

Measured on the 13 logs a push would upload now (83 MB uncompressed, 21 MB gzipped), with no network: the CDN and wrangler are stubbed, with made-up latencies of 0.15 s per CDN request plus 0.05 s per MB and 2 s per wrangler put. The scan before the puts took 13.6 s of CPU without the caches, the same as the old code (14.0 s); from check's caches it takes 0.04 s. The network part took 31.9 s one log at a time, 26.5 s at the default of 4 logs with 1 put, and 14.4 s or 9.6 s with 2 or 4 puts. Under these assumptions, the upload stage of a push goes from about 45 s to about 26.5 s, or 10 s with concurrent puts. The real latencies were not measured, since nothing here may talk to R2 or the CDN. The cold check after this edit took 104 s and reported 0 errors, 8 warnings and 30 notes, as before. Tests: test_performance 63, including new Uploads, AtomicWrites and Perf thread tests, all passing; test_review 25 and test_metrics 21 also pass. Uploads compares cmd_upload with the old serial loop (written out in the test) at 1/1, 4/1, 4/3 and 16/16 jobs and puts, on uploads, refusals, warnings, errors, manifests and CDN contents. It also checks that puts stay within their limit, that nothing is scanned or decompressed again from check's caches and everything is under LLM_TRACES_FULL=1, that a mismatched log is never put, the record's states, and that an interrupted run keeps every verified URL. Mutation checks: dropping the name check, lifting the put limit, ignoring LLM_TRACES_FULL, or not recording uploads that finish during an interrupt each make a test fail.

The brief's Progress section is out of date: the second changeset was done in steps 2a-2g of this run, and this is the start of the third.

Deferred for the user: concurrent wrangler puts (LLM_TRACES_PUT_JOBS above 1) are off because every wrangler process shares one OAuth login, and whether several processes refreshing it at once keep it valid cannot be tested without R2. Two ways forward. You could try LLM_TRACES_PUT_JOBS=4 on a push you are making anyway. Or you could create an R2 API token (an S3-compatible access key with Object Read and Write on the llm-traces bucket only) for a reusable S3 client, which would also save Node's start per object. Either would unlock the measured 26.5 s to about 10 s for these 13 logs. The real CDN and R2 latencies also need a real push to measure.

commits.summary: sync.py speed, step 3b: one lock per repository serializes the commands that write, and a journal recovers an interrupted one
commits.body:
The review's architecture asks for one coordinator for jj mutations, manifest finalization, global outputs and garbage collection, with a repository lock, an operation context and a small durable journal, so that later steps can prepare work in the background and interrupted operations are recoverable. Until now nothing stopped two sessions (or a session and the person at a terminal) from running sync, commit or push at once on one repository: both rewrite manifests, describe changes, delete unreferenced snapshots and rebuild the global files. And the commit hook switches the working copy to the commit it records (jj edit) while it syncs; its hook times out at 60 s, and a cold sync takes about 70 s, so a timeout could leave @ on a finished commit, where the next edits would land.

New: Operation in sync.py. Every command that writes (sync, commit, push, upload, unpublish, stamp, allow, review, init, and hook-commit) holds an exclusive flock on a per-repository lock file in ~/.local/state/llm-traces/locks/; check and scan hold it shared, so they never read a sync half done. A command that finds the lock held prints which command holds it (pid, start time) and waits; hook-commit waits at most 15 s and otherwise leaves its commit to the next sync, which stamps it anyway, and it reads @ again once it has the lock. The Stop hook takes no lock: it writes only its own Langfuse cursor. flock is released by the kernel when the holder dies, so a lock is never stale. Each step an interruption would leave half done is written to a journal before it starts and cleared after: hook-commit's switch of the working copy (recorded before the jj edit), commit's describe-to-jj-new, sync's sessions and global files, and push's stages. The next exclusive command recovers what a killed one left: it puts the working copy back if @ is still on the recorded commit (and leaves it alone if anyone moved it), rebuilds the global files after an interrupted sync, and names what an interrupted commit or push left to run again; check and scan only point at it. SIGTERM and SIGHUP now unwind like Ctrl-C, so a hook's timeout puts the working copy back at once. The specification's Workflow section describes it.

Measured: taking and releasing the lock costs 0.11 ms (exclusive) and 0.04 ms (shared); the first journaled step one jj op log call, 11 ms, which the journal records so jj op log can show what an interrupted command did; each further step 0.34 ms. On this repository a cold check (shared, 104 s) and a sync started 2 s after it: the sync printed who held the lock, waited 103.4 s, then ran (71 s, cold because sync.py changed) and both exited 0; the check gave 0 errors and the same 9 warnings as before (the allow-list proposal awaiting the user and public-ip in eight unuploaded logs of this session). Tests: test_performance 71 (8 new in Coordinator: a writer waits for the holder and names it, readers share and exclude writers, a killed holder's lock is free, no self-deadlock when nested, the journal is empty when nothing is under way, the next operation reports an interrupted commit and push, and against a scratch jj repo, hook-commit killed with SIGKILL mid-switch leaves @ on the commit until the next operation starts a new change above it, while SIGTERM puts it back at once with exit 143), test_review 25, test_metrics 21. Four mutations (no journal before the switch, no SIGTERM handler, a shared lock for writers, no recovery) each fail at least one test.

Observed, for a later step: the transcript, scan, check and sync caches are fingerprinted on the tools' whole source, so every sync.py edit costs one cold sync (about 70 s, 65 s of it redaction) and one cold check (about 104 s). Keying them on the parts that decide redaction and scanning would remove that, at the price of reasoning about which code is relevant; it is not done here.

Deferred for the user (unchanged from step 3a): concurrent wrangler puts share one OAuth login, so push puts one log at a time; an R2 API token for an S3-compatible client would allow several at once. Real CDN and R2 latencies were not measured, since nothing here talks to the network.
